reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC guidelines
clinicalPearls: Characterised by prominent left ventricular trabeculations and deep intertrabecular recesses, giving a two-layered myocardium with a thin compacted and a thick non-compacted layer
May be asymptomatic or present with the triad of heart failure, arrhythmias, and thromboembolic events
Often first suspected on echocardiography using ratios of non-compacted to compacted myocardium in end-systole
Cardiac MRI provides more precise assessment of trabeculation and can detect associated fibrosis
Can occur in isolation or alongside other congenital heart disease and neuromuscular disorders
A familial pattern is common, so evaluation of relatives and consideration of genetic testing are appropriate
The prominent recesses can promote blood stasis and predispose to intracardiac thrombus formation
Distinguishing pathological noncompaction from benign hypertrabeculation, which is common in healthy hearts, remains a diagnostic challenge
reference.pathophysiology: LVNC is thought to reflect arrest of the normal embryonic process in which the loose, spongy fetal myocardial meshwork compacts into solid muscle. The result is persistence of prominent trabeculae and deep recesses lining the ventricular cavity. This altered architecture can impair contractile function, disturb subendocardial perfusion and predispose to fibrosis, ventricular arrhythmias, and blood stasis within the recesses with consequent thromboembolism. Many cases are genetically determined, overlapping with mutations seen in other cardiomyopathies.
additionalDifferentials: Physiological hypertrabeculation in athletes or pregnancy
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography with measurement of non-compacted to compacted myocardial ratio
Cardiac MRI for trabecular quantification and late gadolinium enhancement
12-lead ECG and ambulatory monitoring for arrhythmia
Assessment of left ventricular systolic function
Evaluation for associated neuromuscular disease when indicated
redFlags: Symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Evidence of systemic embolism or intracardiac thrombus
Family history of sudden cardiac death or cardiomyopathy
reference.prognosis: Outcomes range from a benign incidental finding to progressive heart failure, arrhythmias, and thromboembolism. Prognosis is largely driven by the degree of systolic dysfunction and arrhythmic risk; patients with preserved function and no symptoms may do well, whereas those with impaired ventricles have a course resembling other dilated cardiomyopathies.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosing the condition from trabeculation alone without clinical or functional correlation
Missing associated arrhythmias that carry sudden death risk
Underestimating thromboembolic risk in patients with impaired function
Failing to look for associated congenital or neuromuscular disease
